extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / citizens considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_short: justifying federal militia and taxation powers
extracted.subtask_description: Hamilton's arguments (Federalist Nos. 29–32) justifying why the national government should have power to regulate and call forth the militia and to exercise a general power of taxation; explains limits, safeguards, and practical necessities. Targets evaluation and design of constitutional powers for the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments as check on federal usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: The State governments will, in all possible contingencies, afford complete security against invasions of the public liberty by the national authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures have better means of information, can discover danger at a distance, possess organs of civil power and the confidence of the people, can adopt regular plans of opposition, communicate with each other, and unite resources to protect common liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical extent as security
rubrics_metrics.description: The great extent of the country is a further security [against enterprises of ambitious rulers in the national councils].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the federal army quells resistance in one State, distant States can bring fresh forces; advantages obtained in one place must be abandoned to subdue opposition in others; distance and resources make sustaining despotism across an extensive republic difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military force constrained by national resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the military force must, at all events, be regulated by the resources of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a long time it will not be possible to maintain a large army; as means increase, population and strength increase proportionally — making it impractical for the federal government to raise and keep an army capable of erecting a despotism over a large empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: National power to regulate militia is appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: THE power of regulating the militia, and of commanding its services in times of insurrection and invasion are natural incidents to the duties of superintending the common defense, and of watching over the internal peace of the Confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity in organization and discipline enables mutual intelligence and concert in the field; confiding regulation to the national authority accomplishes desirable uniformity when militia are called into service for public defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform organization and discipline of militia required
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in the organization and discipline of the militia would be attended with the most beneficial effects, whenever they were called into service for the public defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It fits militia sooner to acquire proficiency in military functions essential to usefulness; uniformity can only be accomplished by national direction of organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: State appointment of militia officers as safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: RESERVING TO THE STATES RESPECTIVELY THE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS, AND THE AUTHORITY OF TRAINING THE MILITIA ACCORDING TO THE DISCIPLINE PRESCRIBED BY CONGRESS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because officers are appointed by the States, fears of federal subversion via militia are reduced; state appointment secures preponderating influence of the States over the militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal militia power reduces need for standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the federal government can command the aid of the militia in those emergencies which call for the military arm... it can the better dispense with the employment of a different kind of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An efficacious power over the militia removes inducement and pretext for dangerous standing armies; to render an army unnecessary is a more certain method of preventing its existence than prohibitions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posse comitatus and necessary-and-proper implication
rubrics_metrics.description: A right to pass all laws NECESSARY AND PROPER to execute its declared powers would include that of requiring the assistance of the citizens to the officers who may be intrusted with the execution of those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objection that Constitution lacks provision for calling the posse comitatus is unfounded; the power to require citizen assistance is implied in necessary powers to execute laws (but should be understood within constitutional limits and purpose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of disciplining the whole militia
rubrics_metrics.description: The project of disciplining all the militia of the United States is as futile as it would be injurious, if it were capable of being carried into execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolerable expertness requires time and practice; obliging the great body of yeomanry to frequent drills would be a grievance and public inconvenience — a deduction from productive labor. Reasonable aims: have citizens armed and assembled once or twice a year to ensure readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt select well-trained corps of moderate extent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of the utmost importance that a well-digested plan should... be adopted for the proper establishment of the militia... to the formation of a select corps of moderate extent, upon such principles as will really fit them for service in case of need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumscribing the plan allows an excellent body of well-trained militia ready to take the field; this lessens the call for standing armies and provides security against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as substitute and check on standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: That army can never be formidable to the liberties of the people while there is a large body of citizens, little, if at all, inferior to them in discipline and the use of arms, who stand ready to defend their own rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trained citizen militia provides the best possible security against the dangers of a standing army if it should exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of militia in federal hands is exaggerated
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something so far-fetched and so extravagant in the idea of danger to liberty from the militia... Where in the name of common-sense, are our fears to end if we may not trust our sons, our brothers, our neighbors, our fellow-citizens?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militiamen daily mingle with citizens and share interests; combined with state appointment of officers, there is little reasonable cause to apprehend danger from federal regulation of militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual succor among States is a principal end
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of insurrection, or invasion, it would be natural and proper that the militia of a neighboring State should be marched into another, to resist a common enemy... This mutual succor is, indeed, a principal end of our political association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing the power to afford mutual succor under Union direction avoids supine neglect and delayed responses that would follow reliance on voluntary state action alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government must have general power of taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be interwoven, in the frame of the government, a general power of taxation, in one shape or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power must embrace support for national forces, national civil list, payment of national debts, and all matters calling for disbursements from the national treasury; revenue is the vital principle of the body politic and indispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must be able to procure regular and adequate revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Money is, with propriety, considered as the vital principle of the body politic... A complete power, therefore, to procure a regular and adequate supply of it... may be regarded as an indispensable ingredient in every constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without sufficient revenue a government will either resort to plunder or perish by atrophy; the power to procure revenue should be as full as the resources of the community permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute for requisitions: national taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: What substitute can there be imagined for this ignis fatuus in finance, but that of permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by the ordinary methods of taxation authorized in every well-ordered constitution of civil government?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows requisitions upon States are unreliable and enfeeble the Union; national taxation is the practical remedy to secure steady supplies and prevent discord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject internal/external taxation distinction as basis for federal limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between INTERNAL and EXTERNAL taxation... would violate the maxim of good sense and sound policy, which dictates that every POWER ought to be in proportion to its OBJECT; and would still leave the general government in a kind of tutelage to the State governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting federal taxation to imposts (external) would be insufficient for present and future exigencies; powers must be adequate to objects they are meant to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to create new taxing objects enables borrowing and credit
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of creating new funds upon new objects of taxation, by its own authority, would enable the national government to borrow as far as its necessities might require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of taxation powers assures creditors (foreign and domestic) of the government's capacity to pay; without such authority, borrowing would be limited and costly and public credit undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to ends in government powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A government ought to contain in itself every power requisite to the full accomplishment of the objects committed to its care... every power ought to be commensurate with its object; that there ought to be no limitation of a power destined to effect a purpose which is itself incapable of limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary political axioms: means must match ends; revenue power must be as extensive as necessary to meet national exigencies and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address usurpation via government composition, not by narrowing powers
rubrics_metrics.description: All observations founded upon the danger of usurpation ought to be referred to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than limiting powers broadly out of fear of usurpation, design institutional checks (structure, balance, state governments, public dependence) to secure against encroachment; fictive conjectures about usurpation are unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: States should retain independent ability to raise revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: I am willing here to allow, in its full extent, the justness of the reasoning which requires that the individual States should possess an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise their own revenues for the supply of their own wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even while supporting national taxation, preserve state fiscal independence for local purposes so as to maintain local administration and prevent federal monopoly of resources.
